extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / politically engaged American citizens (ratification-era readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political-argument essays arguing for the ratification of a federal Constitution by explaining how a large republic and union mitigate faction, improve commerce, and enable national defenses. The pieces present principles for constitutional design and the practical advantages of union over disunion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as a safeguard against faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the numerous advantages promised by a well-constructed Union, none deserves to be more accurately developed than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Union's large scale and republican structure are presented as the primary means to 'break and control the violence of faction' without violating liberty. The essay argues that controlling effects (rather than destroying liberty or forcing uniformity of opinion) is the appropriate remedy: enlarge the sphere of representation and increase the variety of interests so that no single faction can concert and execute oppressive schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and diagnosis of faction
rubrics_metrics.description: A faction is 'a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes include the fallibility of reason, the connection of reason with self-interest, and especially 'the various and unequal distribution of property' (creditors vs debtors, landed vs manufacturing vs mercantile interests). The text stresses that these latent causes are intrinsic to human nature and social circumstance and therefore cannot be wholly removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal remedies for faction (remove causes vs control effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing causes would require destroying liberty or enforcing uniformity of opinion—both impracticable or worse than the disease. Therefore the practical design of government should focus on controlling effects through institutional arrangements (representation, size of republic, checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican government (representation) as a cure
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic, where government is delegated to a small number of citizens elected by the rest, refines and enlarges the public views and is more likely to produce guardians of the public weal than pure democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation filters popular views through chosen citizens whose wisdom and patriotism better discern the public interest. However, representation can be subverted by intrigue or corruption, so the structure (size of electorate and sphere) must be chosen to minimize that risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large republic preferable to small for selecting fit representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proportion of fit characters is not less in the large than in the small republic, the former will present a greater option and consequently a greater probability of a fit choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger pool of electors and candidates makes it harder for unworthy candidates to succeed by local cabals; the suffrages of a greater number of citizens are 'more free' and more likely to center on men of merit and established character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper balance in number of representatives (avoid extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a mean: by enlarging too much the number of electors, representatives become too little acquainted with local circumstances; by reducing it too much, representatives become unduly attached to local interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution forms a 'happy combination' by referring great and aggregate interests to the national level and local interests to state legislatures; institutional design must find a middle ground in representative numbers to avoid both ignorance of local concerns and parochialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent (sphere) of the republic reduces likelihood of majority faction
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater number of citizens and extent of territory which may be brought within a republican government makes factious combinations less to be dreaded than in a small society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger and more varied society has more parties and interests, making it less probable that a majority will have a common motive to invade others' rights; coordination and secret concert become more difficult as the number and dispersion increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling effects when a faction becomes a majority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a majority is included in a faction, representative institutions and the extent of the union should be such as to render them unable to concert and carry into effect schemes of oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Union's number and local situation should prevent a majority faction from executing its plans even if they share a passion or interest; moral and religious motives cannot be relied upon as adequate controls in such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of State governments within a federal system
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as the separate organization of the members be not abolished ... though it should be in perfect subordination to the general authority of the union, it would still be, in fact and in theory, an association of states, or a confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed Constitution does not abolish State governments but makes them constituent parts of national sovereignty (e.g., direct representation in the Senate) and leaves them exclusive and important portions of sovereign power; federal design can preserve local institutions while creating effective national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confederate republic as a viable model (Montesquieu/Lycia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC is 'a convention by which several smaller STATES agree to become members of a larger ONE' — an assemblage of societies capable of increasing by means of new associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu's favorable discussion (example of Lycia) shows confederacies can exercise interference in internal administration (appointment of judges and magistrates) and still be considered good models; distinctions between confederacy and consolidation are not absolute and depend on discretion in federal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union increases commercial bargaining power
rubrics_metrics.description: By prohibitory regulations, extending throughout the States, we may oblige foreign countries to bid against each other for the privileges of our markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A united market of millions gives leverage to negotiate commercial privileges (e.g., with Britain or West Indies). Fragmentation would reduce bargaining power and enable foreign nations to manipulate American trade through intermediaries, thereby reducing maritime profits and navigation advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: A federal navy as a national necessity and benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment of a federal navy would enable the United States to create a navy which, though it might not vie with great maritime powers, would be of respectable weight and could be decisive in regional contests (e.g., the West Indies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A navy requires pooled resources (naval stores, timber, iron, seamen) from different regions; union makes a navy feasible earlier than separate states, protects commerce, defends neutrality, and increases diplomatic leverage with European powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain maritime and western rights are national rights
rubrics_metrics.description: There are rights of great moment to the trade of America which are rights of the Union — the fisheries, the navigation of the Western lakes, and to that of the Mississippi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolution of the Confederacy would create delicate questions about these rights and likely resolve them to the disadvantage of the weaker partners; national authority secures shared access and defends common resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free interstate commerce strengthens domestic economy
rubrics_metrics.description: An unrestrained intercourse between the States themselves will advance the trade of each by an interchange of their respective productions ... The veins of commerce in every part will be replenished and will acquire additional motion and vigor from a free circulation of the commodities of every part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity of products across states reduces exposure to local crop failures and market fluctuations, increases variety for export, and makes aggregate commerce more favorable; a unity of commercial as well as political interests results from unity of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disunion risks 'passive commerce' and vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: In a state of disunion ... our commerce would be a prey to the wanton intermeddlings of all nations at war with each other ... The rights of neutrality will only be respected when they are defended by an adequate power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weakness invites depredation and loss of neutral privileges; disunion makes the states vulnerable to foreign meddling and economic predation, causing loss of profits and national dignity.
